title: Duck Decoys
summary: Shinnecock decoy carving connects wetland knowledge, family livelihoods, and living artistry—from reed birds to Charles Sumner Bunn and Lyle G. Smith.
content:
Birds, wetlands, and the carver’s eye

A decoy is a model bird used to attract living birds. Its shape suggests a flock resting or feeding safely. For Shinnecock carvers, making that likeness connects artistry with knowledge of coastal waterfowl.3

The Shinnecock Elders’ 2014 resource catalogue places black ducks, mallards, and mergansers within the community’s waterfowl history. It recalls ancestors making decoys from reeds and describes later carving in cedar, pine, and black walnut. The entry names Charles Sumner Bunn and Lyle G. Smith, connecting older practices with named artists.1

Charles Sumner Bunn: a working artist

Charles Sumner Bunn (1865–1952) made decoys and guided hunters. Shelburne Museum identifies him as Shinnecock-Montauk. Its exhibition includes a black duck bearing client Newbold Leroy Edgar’s ownership brand. A photograph documents Bunn displaying decoys at the 1906 National Sportsmen’s Show in Madison Square Garden.2

His daughter Alice Osceola Bunn Martinez preserved memories of his work. Her grandson, artist David Bunn Martine, carried that family record forward.2 Explore Bunn’s biography for his family, guiding, trustee service, and advocacy.

Giving the work its maker’s name

In 2021, Shelburne Museum reattributed five shorebird decoys to Bunn. Photographs, family testimony, and relationships with the objects’ owners informed its decision.32

A separate dispute concerns carvings historically sold as Eugene Cuffee’s. The East Hampton Star reports researcher Jamie Reason’s case for William H. Bennett and disagreement over earlier pieces. That history makes an object’s documented ownership and attribution important parts of its caption.6

A living family tradition

Lyle G. Smith continues to carve decoys and paint. In his January 2023 Shinnecock Voices profile, Shinnecock writer Christian Weaver describes Lyle’s return to carving while recovering from an injury. His father and grandfather worked as hunting guides, and his uncle Norman was a carver.4

Weaver also introduces Lyle’s mother, painter Gloria Smith, and their shared exhibitions at Southampton Arts Center. Their work shows how individual creativity grows within a family tradition. Ma’s House includes Lyle among its Shinnecock artists.45

Look closely at a decoy

Compare the rounded body, bill, head angle, and painted markings with a living American black duck. Which details make the bird recognizable? Then read the caption: who made it, where was it used, and how did that information survive?

Continue with Charles Sumner Bunn, Alice Bunn Martinez, and Lyle G. Smith’s artist profile.

Reeds, carved wood, and waterfowl knowledge

Black ducks, mallards, and mergansers

The catalogue describes waterfowl returning to Shinnecock shorelines and a decoy tradition using reeds and, later, carved wood. It names Charles Sumner Bunn and Lyle G. Smith among Shinnecock carvers, connecting bird knowledge with artistic skill.7

why_this_matters: A decoy holds more than the likeness of a bird. It connects the wetland, the maker’s trained eye, a family’s livelihood, and the people who remember that work. Naming Native makers and listening to their descendants keeps those histories present when useful objects become collected art.
